articles.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.35942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. articles.title: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.35984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. articles.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.

articles.title: Beautiful landscapes may briefly put the brakes on the brain’s movement system
articles.summary: Beauty has long been described as something that makes us pause and look. Neuroscientists in Italy tested that idea by recording brain activity while people viewed nature photos, and found signs that liked images dampened movement preparation.

articles.title: Early trauma may change how children’s cortisol responses relate to anxiety and behavior problems
articles.summary: Children who experience trauma early in life don’t all develop the same problems. A new study suggests their cortisol response to stress may help predict whether anxiety or acting out becomes more prominent as they grow.

articles.summary: arXiv:2610.36541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognition is implemented by distributed neural populations whose collective activity evolves through structured, low-dimensional state spaces. articles.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
articles.summary: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

articles.title: New study explores how money influences interpretations of the Bible
articles.summary: A large survey of Americans reveals that household income strongly shapes how religious individuals interpret the Bible’s teachings on charity, challenging the long-held idea that faith universally suppresses the desire for systemic economic change.

articles.title: Diets high in fat and sugar are linked to impulsiveness in people with borderline personality disorder
articles.summary: Adults with borderline personality disorder who ate more foods high in fat and sugar tended to be more impulsive and took more risks on a gambling task, though their diets were unrelated to overall symptom severity.

articles.title: A mirror trick that adds a sixth finger also changes what people think their hand can grab
articles.summary: With a mirror and some well-timed brushstrokes, researchers gave volunteers the sensation of a sixth finger. Afterward, people judged that their hand needed a wider opening to fit through and could grasp larger blocks.

articles.title: Intelligence and fertility: Do smarter people have fewer children? The strongest evidence suggests a smaller, more complicated link
articles.summary: People with higher intelligence scores tend to have slightly smaller families in American and British surveys. But when researchers wait until people finish having children and compare brothers from the same families, the link shrinks or even reverses.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work
